561.title: Guru Angad's voice
561.hook: many saloks in the var are Guru Angad's, marked mahala 2
561.howItsDone: Sikhs read the mahala heading above each composition in the Guru Granth Sahib to know which Guru wrote it, and Guru Angad's saloks are sung within Asa di Var and other vars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pauri, and your line: step by step. We saw that some saloks beside the pauris aren't Guru Nanak's. Today, whose they are.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' hymns are signed the same way: Nanak, in the closing lines, page after page. But Guru Nanak didn't write all of them. The later Gurus whose words are in the Granth also signed as Nanak. So how does a reader know who's speaking? A small label at the top of each composition: mahala, and a number. Mahala one, Guru Nanak. Mahala five, Guru Arjan. In the Asa di Var, every so often, the label reads mahala two. You've already heard that voice three times this block.
screen: `HYMN AFTER HYMN SIGNED: NANAK.` → `A LABEL AT THE TOP: MAHALA.` → `MAHALA TWO.`

segments.voice: Mahala two is Guru Angad, the second Guru. Before that he was Bhai Lehna, a devoted man from a village in Punjab who came to Guru Nanak at Kartarpur and stayed. Guru Nanak named him his successor and gave him a new name, Angad, which Sikhs often explain as ang, limb: a part of the Guru's own body. He left no long hymns in the Granth. What it holds of his is a set of saloks, many of them inside vars, beside Guru Nanak's pauris. Why sign as Nanak? Sikhs understand the Guruship as one light passing from body to body, the way one lamp lights another. Guru Angad isn't borrowing a name. In Sikh understanding it's the same light, speaking again; mahala two simply tells you which lamp. You've met that voice in this var. A hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru: mahala two, on day five hundred thirty-nine. Ego as a chronic illness with its medicine inside it: mahala two. The servant who argues: mahala two again. Listen across them and a voice emerges: short, practical, often about the Guru, about ego, about how a disciple actually behaves. It sounds like someone who spent years as a student before he became a teacher, and never forgot it. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Angad for teaching children, keeping the langar going, encouraging the Gurmukhi script and, some accounts say, for the wrestling ground. His saloks are the quiet second voice in the dawn song.
screen: `MAHALA TWO: GURU ANGAD.` · `ANG: A LIMB OF THE GURU.` · `ONE LIGHT, A SECOND LAMP.` · `SHORT, PRACTICAL, A STUDENT'S VOICE.` · then, large: `THE SECOND VOICE.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka or an app, open the Asa di Var, look at the small headings, salok mahala one, salok mahala two, and read one marked two slowly. If you can't look it up, say one from this block once: the medicine is within. Notice how it sounds from a man who was first a student, and if you pray, say Waheguru.
Bhai Lehna, the name Guru Angad carried before he became Guru: his saloks, marked mahala two, are short, practical verses signed Nanak because, in Sikh understanding, it is one light.
Your line: the second voice. One light, a second lamp. That's day five hundred sixty-one.

562.title: Singing it at dawn
562.hook: the full var with chhants takes about three hours at dawn
562.howItsDone: In gurdwaras that keep the morning order, ragis sing Asa di Var around dawn, weaving Guru Ram Das's chhants between the saloks and pauris; the full form can take around three hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Lehna: Guru Angad, whose saloks are the second voice in the var. Today we leave the page and go where the Asa di Var actually lives: in the air, before sunrise.

It's still dark. The streets are empty except for a milk truck and a few people walking quickly, heads covered. Inside the gurdwara the lights are low and the floor is cool. The Guru Granth Sahib has been opened for the day. A few dozen people sit cross-legged on white sheets, some in shawls, some with children asleep against them. At the front, the ragis, the musicians, tune a harmonium and tap the tabla once. Then they begin a song that won't finish until the sky is fully light.
screen: `STILL DARK, STREETS EMPTY.` → `WHITE SHEETS, LOW LIGHTS.` → `A SONG UNTIL FULL LIGHT.`

segments.voice: In gurdwaras that keep the old morning order, the Asa di Var is sung every morning, in the hours around dawn, as part of the day's first kirtan. It has long been a fixed part of the morning program. It's sung in Rag Asa, to the old tune we met on day five hundred thirty-seven, the ballad of a king. But what the sangat hears is longer than what you'd read in the Granth. The ragis weave in the chhants of Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru: twenty-four stanzas from his chhants in Rag Asa, one for each pauri. So it goes something like this: a chhant of Guru Ram Das, sung slowly and lovingly; then the saloks; then Guru Nanak's pauri, gathering it all into a step; then the next chhant. Sung in full, it can take around three hours. Some gurdwaras sing a shorter form, a few chhants or all of them, depending on the day and the ragis. Why dawn? Gurbani calls the hours before sunrise amrit vela, the ambrosial time, and Japji speaks of meditating on the true Name and its greatness in those early hours. The mind hasn't filled up yet. The phone hasn't started. And there's something about hearing wonder, awe, ego and sweetness sung while the sky goes from black to gray to gold. The var you've been studying word by word was never meant to stay on the page. It was meant to be sung, slowly, with the sun coming up behind it.
screen: `SUNG EACH MORNING IN RAG ASA.` · `GURU RAM DAS'S CHHANTS WOVEN IN.` · `CHHANT, SALOKS, PAURI, AGAIN.` · `AMRIT VELA: THE AMBROSIAL HOURS.` · then, large: `BEFORE SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: Picture fifteen minutes before tomorrow's sunrise: where you'd sit, and what you'd hear, a recording of the Asa di Var or simply the quiet, while the window lightens. Breathe slowly as you picture the color changing from black to gray to gold. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
Amrit vela, the ambrosial hours before dawn: the Asa di Var is sung through them, Guru Ram Das's chhants woven between the saloks and pauris.
Your line: before sunrise. The var was made for the hour the sky changes. Until tomorrow.

563.title: Asa di Var close
563.hook: wonder, awe, sweetness, the thread of compassion
563.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Asa di Var sung in gurdwaras each morning, followed by Ardas and karah prashad, and many carry a favorite salok from it through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit vela, the ambrosial hours when the Asa di Var is sung. Today we close it: four weeks of the dawn ballad, gathered like a pauri.

When the dawn singing ends, the sangat doesn't scatter right away. People stand for Ardas. Karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is passed hand to hand. Someone folds the white sheets. Outside, the sun is up and the streets are filling with buses and school uniforms. People walk out carrying almost nothing: no notes, no book. Maybe one line, still humming in the back of the head. That's one way the var travels: as lines people carry out the door.
screen: `ARDAS, AND KARAH PRASHAD.` → `THE SUN FULLY UP.` → `ONE LINE CARRIED OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Let's walk the staircase once, from the top. An old ballad of heroes, given new words and sung to a king's tune. A sacrifice to the Guru a hundred times a day, the Guru who made angels out of men. A hundred moons, and still dark without the Guru. The One who made Himself and watches with delight. Then four steps of seeing: vismaad, wonder at every sound and color; kudrat, power in seeing, eating, loving; bhau, the wind and rivers moving in awe; and nirbhau, nirankar, only the Formless without fear. Then the people: the contented ones who served. Haumai, ego as a chronic illness with its medicine inside it. Cartloads of books, and only one thing counted. Koorh, the false king and everything that passes. Sach, truth known only when the heart is true. Then the turnings: pain the medicine, pleasure the disease. Mitthat neevee, sweetness and humility, the heavy side of the scale. The silk-cotton tree, tall and useless. The sacrifice to the Guru who put wisdom on the eyes. Then the thread: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist; a thread that won't break, burn, stain or be lost. Sootak moved inside: greed, lies, coveting, gossip. Fikka words that make a fikka life. The servant who argues. And the shape itself: pauris as steps, Guru Angad's second voice, the whole thing sung as the sky turns gold. If one thread runs through it all, it might be the one in the carry. The var keeps starting with wonder. Before it corrects anyone, it makes them look. Wonder first, then the work.
screen: `THE BALLAD, THE GURU, THE MOONS.` · `WONDER, POWER, AWE, THE FEARLESS.` · `EGO, KOORH, TRUTH, SWEETNESS.` · `THE THREAD, THE SERVANT, THE DAWN.` · then, large: `WONDER AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Let the block pass through your mind once more, bhau, the simmal, the scale, the thread, dal without salt, the arguing servant, and wait for the one that keeps coming back. Say its picture to yourself in one sentence, then breathe with it, the way the sangat carries a line out the door. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
Vismaad, wonder: twenty-four pauris and their saloks, sung at dawn, hold vismaad, awe, truth, sweetness, and the thread of compassion.
Your line: wonder at dawn. One line, carried out the door, is plenty. Four weeks of the dawn ballad, complete.

564.title: A year of longing
564.hook: an old Punjabi form: twelve months, each colored by longing for the Beloved
564.howItsDone: Gurdwaras that observe sangrand, the first day of each solar month, read that month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; some Sikhs do not mark the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Asa di Var with your line: wonder at dawn. The dawn ballad began in wonder. Today a new part of the path begins, and this one begins in longing.

Being apart from someone you love changes the calendar. The first cold morning reminds you of their coat. A summer storm reminds you of the porch where you watched one together. A festival comes, and there's an empty chair. The seasons keep pointing at who isn't there. Folk singers in Punjab turned that feeling into a song form, already old, tradition says, when the Gurus took it up: a woman whose beloved is far away, singing her way through the year, one month at a time.
screen: `THE FIRST COLD MORNING.` → `THE SEASONS POINT AT WHO ISN'T THERE.` → `A SONG THROUGH THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: It's called barah maha. Barah is twelve, maha is months. In the folk songs, each month has its weather and its work: the heat of one, the rains of another, the harvest, the festivals. In each, the woman sings how the season sharpens her missing. The rain falls and he isn't here. The swings go up in the trees and he isn't here. Two Gurus turned this folk form toward the One. Guru Nanak wrote a Barah Maha in Rag Tukhari, near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, wrote one in Rag Majh, on ang 133, and that's the one we'll walk through, month by month. In Gurbani, the beloved far away isn't a husband off at war or trade. It's the One, and the woman singing is the soul. That image, the soul as a bride longing for the divine Husband, runs all through the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs of every gender sing it as their own. The form's power is that it doesn't save longing for special days. It finds it in the ordinary turn of the calendar. Each month has its own color of missing, so each month becomes a chance to remember. Gurdwaras that mark sangrand, the first day of the solar month, read that month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; some Sikhs keep the day and others don't. Where it's kept, the calendar on the wall becomes a calendar of longing too.
screen: `BARAH MAHA: TWELVE MONTHS.` · `EACH SEASON SHARPENS THE MISSING.` · `THE BELOVED IS THE ONE.` · `READ ON SANGRAND, MONTH BY MONTH.` · then, large: `EVERY MONTH A LONGING.`

segments.voice: Ask what this month is like where you are, the light, the temperature, what's growing or dying, what the evenings smell like, and let one detail come clearly. Then notice whether the month carries any longing, a person, a place, or an ache you can't quite name, and let the season and the longing sit together without fixing either. If you pray, you can say Waheguru.
Barah Maha. The twelve months: an old Punjabi song form where each season colors the longing for an absent beloved. In Gurbani, the Beloved is the One.
Your line: every month a longing. Twelve months, twelve colors of missing. Day five hundred sixty-four, counted.

565.title: Separated by our deeds
565.hook: separated by our own deeds, we ask the Lord in mercy to unite us (Barah Maha, ang 133)
565.howItsDone: Sikhs read the opening stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha before the months, and its plea for reunion is heard whenever the Barah Maha is sung or read on sangrand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Barah Maha: twelve months, each with its own color of longing. Before Guru Arjan names a single month, he opens with a stanza about the separation itself.

Two old friends stop talking. Nobody can quite remember when. There wasn't a big fight. Just a missed call, a canceled plan, a comment taken the wrong way, a year of not reaching out. Each small choice made sense at the time. Then one day you realize there's a distance between you that you built yourselves, one brick at a time. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha begins exactly there: not with a month, but with how the distance got there, and who can close it.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS STOP TALKING.` → `NO BIG FIGHT, JUST SMALL CHOICES.` → `A DISTANCE WE BUILT OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: The opening stanza, on ang 133, in paraphrase: we are separated by the deeds we have done. Have mercy, Lord, and unite us with yourself. Kirat karam ke veechhurhe. Kirat is what has been done; karam is action; veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart. The stanza is honest about how it happened. Nobody else did it to us; our own doings built the distance. Yet the very next breath isn't despair. It's a request: kar kirpaa, have mercy. Unite us. Then Guru Arjan paints the tiredness: wandering in the four corners and the ten directions, we've grown weary and come to your sanctuary. And he reaches for two farm pictures every Punjabi listener would know. A cow that gives no milk is of no use. A crop without water withers and won't fetch a price. Life without the One, he's saying, is like that: dry, unproductive, missing its whole point. Without meeting the beloved Friend, where can anyone find rest? The homes and towns where the Beloved isn't present are like burning furnaces. Each month to come will have its own color, but the root is here: separation by our own deeds, and a longing only grace can meet. Notice the balance. The stanza doesn't excuse us; the distance is ours. But it doesn't ask us to close it alone, either. In Sikh teaching, both are true at once: we're responsible for our deeds, and reunion comes by the One's grace.
screen: `KIRAT KARAM: WHAT WE HAVE DONE.` · `HAVE MERCY, UNITE US.` · `A COW WITHOUT MILK, A CROP WITHOUT WATER.` · `OUR DEEDS, AND THE ONE'S GRACE.` · then, large: `UNITE US.`

segments.voice: Think of one distance in your life you helped build, with a person, with a part of yourself or, if this is your language, with God, and without arguing whose fault it was, just admit your bricks. Then let the opposite feeling come: a wish to close it. If you pray, hold the stanza's own request, kar kirpaa, have mercy; if you don't, simply hold the wish.
Veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart: the opening of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha says we are veechhurhe by what we've done, and ask the One in mercy to unite us.
Your line: unite us. It's a humble request, not a verdict. See you in the month of Chet.

566.title: The month of Chet
566.hook: in Chet, remember the Lord and great joy comes (Barah Maha, ang 133)
566.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Chet, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Chet stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the Nanakshahi calendar Chet is the first month of the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, veechhurhe: separated by our own deeds, and asking in mercy to be united. Today the year begins, with the first month and its spring.

The cold has finally gone. Mustard fields that were yellow all winter are going to seed. Wheat is turning gold and heavy, a few weeks from harvest. Trees push out new leaves overnight, and the koel, a bird with a rising call, starts singing in the mornings. This is Chet, roughly March into April in Punjab, when everything seems to come back. And Guru Arjan begins his year of longing here, in the season when you'd think nobody has any reason to long for anything.
screen: `THE COLD GONE, WHEAT GOING GOLD.` → `CHET: MARCH INTO APRIL IN PUNJAB.` → `LONGING IN THE SEASON OF PLENTY.`

segments.voice: Chet is the first month in Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and the Nanakshahi calendar begins its year with Chet too. The stanza on ang 133 opens, in paraphrase: in Chet, by worshiping the Lord of the universe, a deep and lasting joy arises. Then it says how. Meeting the holy ones, the One is found, and the tongue repeats the Name. Those who have found their Lord, their coming into the world is counted. To live even a moment without the One is to waste a life. The One is present in water, on land, in the sky and in the forests, and those who don't keep the One in mind suffer much pain. It closes with a wish: I touch the feet of whoever brings me to meet that Lord in Chet. Notice the joy. It isn't the joy of the season, the sunshine and new leaves. It's the joy of remembering. Spring is everywhere, in water, land, sky and forest, because the One is everywhere in it, so the green outside becomes a reminder of what's inside it. Some Punjabi listeners also hear a play of sounds. Chet is the month, but chet is also an everyday word for awareness, for keeping something in mind, as in chete, remembering. The stanza never says it's a pun, so it's only a sound worth noticing. In the season when the world wakes up, the soul is asked to wake up too.

As you picture it, breathe slowly and think of one thing in you that's been waiting to grow, and let the seed hold that wish. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over it.
Chet. Spring, the first month of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha: remembering the One brings deep joy, and the One fills water, land, sky and forest.
Your line: chet: joy. It comes from remembering, not from the weather. Day five hundred sixty-six: spring has started.

567.title: The month of Vaisakh
567.hook: in Vaisakh, how can the separated be patient (Barah Maha, ang 133)
567.howItsDone: On the sangrand of Vaisakh, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Vaisakh stanza of the Barah Maha, and Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi in this month, remembering the founding of the Khalsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chet: joy that comes from remembering the One. That closes a week: Bhai Lehna, the dawn singing, the var's close, the year of longing, veechhurhe, Chet. Today the second month, and the ache gets sharper.
screen: `CHET: JOY.` · `A WEEK: THE DAWN VAR ENDS, THE MONTHS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Vaisakh is harvest month in Punjab, April into May. The wheat is cut and threshed, the grain goes to market, and for a farming family it's a well-fed, busy, crowded time. Fairs come to the villages. Vaisakhi, the festival, falls in this month, and for Sikhs it carries the memory of the Vaisakhi when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa. Everyone is home, celebrating. And in the folk songs, that's what makes it a hard month to be the one whose beloved is missing.
screen: `HARVEST, APRIL INTO MAY.` → `VAISAKHI, AND THE KHALSA.` → `A HARD MONTH TO BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: The Vaisakh stanza on ang 133 opens with a question. In paraphrase: in Vaisakh, how can the brides be patient, the ones separated from love? Dheeran, patience, steadiness. How do you hold steady when everyone around you is with the one they love? Then Guru Arjan names why she's alone. She has forgotten the Lord, the true Friend, and clung to maya, the world's deceptive glitter. And he names what she clings to: sons, wife, wealth, none of which go along with you at the end. Only the One is imperishable. Entangled in false busy-ness, the whole world is wearing itself out. Notice the timing. The grain is in. The money's coming. Guru Arjan isn't against any of that; Sikhs are householders, and earning honestly is part of the path. But the fullest month of the year is also an easy month to forget the One entirely. Plenty can be loud. Then the stanza turns. Vaisakh becomes beautiful, it says, when a holy person brings you to meet the Lord. The same harvest, festival and crowded house become lovely once the missing one is found. So the ache isn't the end. It's the door. Longing is a kind of compass needle: it points to what's missing, and a person who never felt it might never look. Vaisakh is the month of having almost everything, and the stanza asks gently what the almost is.
screen: `HOW CAN THE SEPARATED BE PATIENT?` · `CLINGING TO MAYA, FORGETTING THE FRIEND.` · `PLENTY CAN BE LOUD.` · `BEAUTIFUL WHEN THE LORD IS MET.` · then, large: `VAISAKH: LONGING.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind whose absence you feel, someone living and reachable you haven't spoken to in too long, and picture their voice. Feel the missing plainly, the way the stanza does, and hold their face for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.
Vaisakh. Harvest and festival, when the separated bride can't hold steady, and the month becomes beautiful only when the Beloved is met.
Your line: vaisakh: longing. The ache is a door, not the end. On to the heat tomorrow.
